img-p126-1.draft: The GRADE approach to rating confidence in an estimate of effect. Rows give study design — randomized controlled trials, which start at high confidence, and observational studies, which start at low. Between them, five reasons for lowering confidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and three for raising it (large effect, dose response, and plausible confounding that would either reduce a demonstrated effect or suggest a spurious one). The right-hand column gives the four resulting levels — high, moderate, low and very low — each shown with the circle notation, from four filled circles down to one.

img-p154-1.saw: a comparison table of four rapid-review types
img-p154-1.draft: A comparison of four types of rapid review — a traditional systematic review conducted rapidly, a rapid review of systematic reviews, a rapid review of systematic reviews plus primary studies, and a rapid review of primary studies only — across twelve methodological dimensions. The traditional review allows up to 16 weeks where the three rapid forms allow up to 12. It differs from them throughout: no restrictions on literature search or number of databases against restrictions and 2–3 databases; complete data-extraction verification against one reviewer with selected verification; outcomes restricted to four or fewer against two to four with more if available. Rows also cover question types, number of questions, use of systematic reviews, grey literature, screening, study designs included, risk-of-bias assessment, and assessment of the quality of the body of evidence.

vfig-p034.saw: Fig 14, the DHSC architecture: services, interoperability layer and supply-chain systems with explanatory callouts
vfig-p034.draft: Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. vfig-p041.saw: Fig 20, transactional data from a supply-chain flow rising through the interoperability layer into analytics services, with the questions they answer
vfig-p041.draft: Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

vfig-p049.saw: Fig 23, total cost of ownership grouped into implement, scale, operate and ongoing cost components; the crop also takes in the Step 3 text panel above it
vfig-p049.draft: Fig 23, 'Cost components to determine the total cost of ownership'. A dashed loop labelled 'Total cost of ownership' encloses four groups of cost components. IMPLEMENT: sourcing (RFP, RFI, RFQ), software, hardware and infrastructure, design and development, integration and interoperability, testing and training, and deployment. SCALE: expansion of deployment, training, and hardware and infrastructure. OPERATE: software subscriptions, maintenance (personnel, software, hardware), ongoing training, and monitoring and evaluation. ONGOING: management, governance and overhead. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

vfig-p055.saw: Fig 24, supply-chain systems at each location exchanging data through the interoperability layer with traceability services; the page's 'Fig. 25' is a cross-reference
vfig-p055.draft: Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

vfig-p056.saw: Fig 25, a mock track-and-trace screen for one batch above the event flow that feeds it
vfig-p056.draft: Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.

vfig-p014.saw: Fig. 5, the SMART Guidelines five-layer diagram with localisation and an evidence feedback loop
vfig-p014.draft: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines Approach'. A research and evidence base feeds five knowledge layers and their products: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each passes through LOCALISATION into a country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures, localised requirements, localised machine-readable code and standards, localised static digital services, and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. All feed DATA, EVIDENCE, AND IMPACT, which returns to the evidence base as EVIDENCE FROM DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS.

vfig-p015.saw: Fig. 6, an ANC BPMN swimlane workflow with an enlarged inset of its assessment and counselling activities, some highlighted
vfig-p015.draft: Fig. 6, 'Example of an Antenatal Care Business clinical workflow with highlighted' activities. The upper part is a swimlane process in a health facility, with Client and Health worker lanes. The client arrives at the facility, then goes through registration, rapid assessment and management, a danger-signs/referral decision, pregnancy confirmation, a first-contact decision and a quick check. These lead to collecting the woman's profile and history, then an ANC assessment (check symptoms and follow-up, conduct physical exam, conduct laboratory tests and imaging), then 10. Counselling, in-facility management and treatment, with subactivities 10.1 to 10.9, then a referral decision, scheduling, and self-care in the home or community until the woman returns. The lower part enlarges activities 6 to 10. Highlighted borders mark 9 (conduct laboratory tests and imaging), 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis — the activities that involve health products.

vfig-p028.draft: Fig. 8, 'Linkage across classifications, generic products and trade items'. vfig-p029.saw: Fig. 9, a three-class data model with attribute cardinalities and 1-to-0..* associations
vfig-p029.draft: Fig. 9, 'Relationship between generic product, trade item and regulated trade item'. Three classes are drawn as boxes listing their attributes with cardinalities. GENERIC PRODUCT has identifier 0..*, status, name (nameType, nameValue), description, classification, unitOfUse, dosageForm, strength, routeOfAdministration, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, doseQuantity, attribute (type, value[x]) and associatedProduct (product, relationship, quantity). TRADE ITEM has identifier 1..*, status, tradeItemName, description, classification, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, associatedGenericProduct (genericProduct, quantity), contains (tradeItem, quantity) and attribute. REGULATED TRADE ITEM has identifier, status, jurisdiction, authorisationHolder, validityPeriod, authorisedTradeItem, attribute and associatedProduct. The associations read: one generic product to zero or more trade items, and one trade item to zero or more regulated trade items.

vfig-p043.draft: Fig. 3.1, 'Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges' and requirements. Three columns. BUSINESS PROCESS ANALYSIS, 'Think — how do we do our work now?': define goals and objectives, determine the health programme processes to target, map the user journey and workflow, and identify pain points. BUSINESS PROCESS REDESIGN, 'Rethink — how should we do our work now?': examine tasks and workflow, identify inefficiencies, restructure them, and select digital health interventions for the prioritized health system challenges. REQUIREMENTS DEFINITION, 'Describe — how can an information system support our work?': define the tasks for the optimized processes, describe how business rules are implemented, check that the enabling environment can support the interventions, define what the interventions should do from end-user needs, and determine whether existing ICT systems can be leveraged.

vfig-p035.draft: Fig. 9, 'Example business process matrix from family planning DAK'. A Registration (FP.A), with client and clerk or health-care provider, ensures the client is in the system and queued for counselling; its tasks are to search for, review and update, or create a client record. B Family planning counselling (FP.B), with client and health-care provider, discusses methods and selects one the client is medically eligible for; its tasks run from taking a history and a risk assessment through checking medical eligibility criteria and stock to referral if the facility cannot provide the method. vfig-p042.saw: Fig. 12, a three-question flow with explanation and action columns
vfig-p042.draft: Fig. 12, 'Is each and every data element collected truly needed?'. Three rows, each reading Question → Explanation → Action to be taken, with arrows chaining each row's action into the next question. 1. Is the data element duplicated? Duplicates may share a definition under different labels, or be collected on several forms; reconcile them into one element collected once. 2. Is the data element needed for service delivery or accountability? Ask whether it supports clinical decision-making, mandatory reporting or accountability; if not, consider removing it to reduce the data-entry burden on health workers. 3. Is the data element orphaned? Orphaned data is hard to use without its context; link it to its primary data elements (anything not needed will already have gone at question 2).

vfig-p045.draft: Fig. 13, 'Example decision-support logic matrix from DAK for HIV'. A table with four columns: activity ID and name, decision table ID, decision table description, and reference/source. It has six rows, HIV.DT.01 to HIV.DT.06: check for serious illness; test for HIV using the testing algorithm; determine retest recommendation; PrEP eligibility check; determine PEP or PrEP regimen; and screen for TB. Each row cites the WHO consolidated guideline section it is drawn from — for example the 2019 consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, and its figures on universal HIV testing and early infant diagnosis. vfig-p046.saw: Fig. 14, a branching decision tree from antenatal registration on HIV status and risk
vfig-p046.draft: Fig. 14, 'Decision-support logic for a clinical care pathway in the form of a decision tree'. It starts at 'Antenatal registration — provider-initiated HIV testing & counselling' and splits on the result. HIV-positive leads to PMTCT, treatment, support and an offer of partner notification, then partner testing. Partner HIV-negative leads to reassessing the woman's risk and offering partner referral for VMMC. Partner not tested or HIV-positive leads to offering the partner HIV treatment (if positive), condom promotion and risk-reduction counselling. HIV-negative leads to standard post-test guidance and counselling on prevention, then two branches: offer partner testing and a risk assessment (which feeds partner testing), and a risk assessment using a tool. That tool separates a woman at substantial risk of HIV acquisition from one who is not. At substantial risk, she is offered comprehensive prevention options — STI screening and treatment, condom promotion, risk-reduction counselling, PrEP with emphasis on adherence, and follow-up ANC visits. A woman who chooses to initiate PrEP then receives clinical laboratory assessments, adherence counselling, and emphasis on follow-up visits and repeat HIV testing. Source: WHO (29).

vfig-p054.saw: Fig. 15, three coloured phases on fidelity-versus-time axes with questions under each
vfig-p054.draft: Fig. 15, 'Levels of insight gained from different prototypes'. The vertical axis is level of prototype fidelity and the horizontal axis is the time required to develop the protocol. An arrow climbs through three phases: Validation, with low-fidelity prototypes (sketches, wireframes); Refinement, with moderate-fidelity prototypes (mockups); and Deployment, with higher-fidelity prototypes (clickable prototypes). Under each phase are the questions it answers. Validation asks: do users need this, and would this digital record solve their administrative reporting problems? Refinement asks: could it improve service delivery or accountability, and will users use it as intended? Deployment asks: does it have the key features, will users adopt it, and what behaviour change or roadblocks to adoption must be addressed? Adapted from Norman Tran/Stanford school (35).

vfig-p013.saw: Fig. 1, health content plus digital health interventions plus digital applications, above a foundational-layer grid
vfig-p013.draft: Fig. 1, 'Digital adaptation kits representing health content within broader needs for digital health implementations'. Three boxes are joined by plus signs: HEALTH CONTENT (information aligned with recommended health practices or validated health content), shown with the cover of this kit; DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS (a discrete function of digital technology to achieve health-sector objectives); and DIGITAL APPLICATIONS (ICT systems and communication channels that facilitate delivery of the interventions and content). An orange frame encloses the three, and dotted lines run from it to the highlighted 'Services and applications' cell of a Foundational Layer (ICT and enabling environment) below, whose other cells are leadership and governance, strategy and investment, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation, policy and compliance, and workforce. Source: adapted from reference 14.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 2, the five SMART layers L1-L5 on the left, each feeding a country L1-L5 adaptation on the right through a localisation bar
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 2, 'Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum'. Five rows: L1 Narrative (narrative guidelines: evidence-based recommendations with implementation and data guidance); L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits: software-neutral documentation of operational and functional requirements such as personas, workflows, metadata, algorithms, minimum data sets and priority metrics); L3 Machine readable (structured software-neutral specifications, code, terminology and interoperability standards); L4 Executable (reference software that executes static algorithms and interoperable components); and L5 Dynamic (precision health models trained and optimised with advanced analytics). Each row passes through a vertical 'Localisation' bar to its country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures; localised requirements; localised machine-readable code and standards; localised static digital services within a digital health enterprise; and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. A blue arrow beside them runs from 'Paper systems' at the top to 'Smart digital systems' at the bottom. Source: adapted from reference 18.

vfig-p024.saw: Fig. 3, seven coloured phases with their steps, beside a grid of resource tiles
vfig-p024.draft: Fig. 3, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases, each with its steps: 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling. Beside them a grid of tiles names resources for each phase, marked as PDF for print or online environment; among them the WHO-ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), WHO guideline recommendations on digital interventions, Open Health Information Exchange, TOGAF, and a highlighted tile 'WHO SMART guidelines: digital adaptation kits (this document) and machine-readable recommendations' in phase 05. Source: adapted from WHO (reference 1).

vfig-p036.saw: Figure 3, a four-lane Continuity of Care workflow with every path shown
vfig-p036.draft: Figure 3, 'Continuity of Care scenario': the vaccine is administered, the core data set is recorded on the DDCC paper certificate, and the record is then made available in digital form. Four lanes: subject of care, vaccinator, data entry personnel, DDCC holder. (1) The subject of care arrives at the care site; (2) the vaccinator vaccinates and (3) records core data set elements on a paper certificate, which the holder receives as Point A, a paper record of DDCC:VS. Is there a digital health solution at the care site? If no, (5) data entry personnel record the elements in a digital health solution. If yes, (4) the vaccinator records them in one; then, does the care site have Internet connectivity? Yes leads directly, and no via step 5, to Point B: the record of vaccination status is available in a digital form. End.

vfig-p046.saw: Figure 7, five services joined by labelled arrows, some dashed and optional
vfig-p046.draft: Figure 7, 'The relationships between digital services for Proof of Vaccination'. A digital health solution submits a vaccination event to the DDCC:VS generation service, which returns a DDCC:VS. The HCID is provided by an existing national system or issued by the generation service. vfig-p048.saw: Figure 8, a four-lane Proof of Vaccination workflow with every path shown

vfig-p065.draft: Figure 14, 'How digital signatures work', under the heading Document Signing. A signer starts from a document (vaccination data); a hash is calculated from the document, giving the document hash; the hash is digitally signed with a private key, giving the signed hash; the signed hash is added to the document, giving a document with a digitally signed hash (the DDCC:VS).

vfig-p066.saw: Figure 15, the signing flow above a validation flow
vfig-p066.draft: Figure 15, 'How digital signature verification works'. The upper panel, Document Signing, repeats Figure 14: document, document hash, signed with the private key, signed hash added to the document to make the DDCC:VS. The signer sends the digitally signed document and the public key to the verifier. The lower panel, Document Validation: the verifier calculates a hash from the document and, using the public key, obtains the hash from the signed hash; the two values are compared, and a matching hash indicates a valid document, one that contains the information that was signed with the private key.
